newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - March 19.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - March 19.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Following speculation by Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan that "outside influences" had inspired Monday's attempted military revolt in the country, Australian Prime Minister John Howard repeated warnings against the use of hired mercenaries on Bougainville, saying possible Australian aid cuts would not be ruled out. Page 1.
Over six years ahead of schedule, the High Court's leading conservative, Justice Sir Daryl Dawson, is to resign in August.

Dawson's resignation creates a surprise opportunity for the Federal Government to entrench conservative dominance of the High Court in its first term of office, as Chief Justice Sir Gerard Brennan will stand down in 10 months as he reaches the statutory retirement age of 70. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard yesterday struggled to calm his backbench, dismissing concerns about the new superannuation surcharge and insisting on an end to backbench lobbying to retain existing car tariff levels. The Government is also having trouble with backbench rural MPs over the Wik native title case. Page 3.

Australian Bureau of Statistics figures released yesterday showed that working days lost last year because of striking workers rose to just under one million, an increase of 69 per cent. The figures were the highest for four years, but were still lower tan those recorded during the industrial troubles of the 1991 recession.
Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Prime Minister John Howard has supported his Papua New Guinean counterpart Sir Julius Chan's sacking of defence head Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, who stood down without fuss after urging his troops to support their new commander. However, Howard is till unhappy at Chan's insistence to use mercenaries in the Bougainville conflict, and says the situation on the island will be aggravated by the use of such action.
Page 1.

As official records revealed Independent Senator Mal Colston received more than A$148,000 in benefits for almost 100 overnight stays, the embattled Senator has been asked to explain the discrepancies. Colston headed a list of figures of travel allowance payouts tabled in the Senate yesterday at his request, but at least nine other Senators claimed between A$90,000 and A$120,000 in the same period. Page 1.

As Prime Minister John Howard and Federal Treasurer Peter Costello have agreed in principle to apply more rigorously the foreign investment rules for Australia's media ownership, the control of the Channel Ten television network could be affected, with Canadian company CanWest expected to be forced to sell most of its holding. Page 1.

Australian cricket captain Mark Taylor was not affected by two more failures with the bat in the second cricket Test in South Africa yesterday as he happily revelled in what he described as the "biggest Test match win I've played in". As speculation contnues about Taylor's future, he admitted he is frustrated with his form, but wishes to remain captain for as long as he can. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

A report obtained by the Herald indicates the Kogarah Council wants to drop its speed limits on all residential roads from 60 kilometres and hour to 40 kilometres an hour. Should the plan go ahead, the Council would be enforcing the lowest speed limits i the Western world. Page 1.

The Perinatal Society of Australia and New Zealand annual congress heard yesterday from childhood cancer expert Professor Bernard Stewart, who said babies that are large at birth and those born with defects are more likely to develop childhood cancers, ye those born to teenage mothers posed a lesser risk. Page 1.

Australian cricket vice-captain Ian Healy was unable to recall much of his second Test-winning six, which placed Australia in an unbeatable 2-0 lead in the Test series against the South African Proteas. Healy hit a six when Australia needed five runs to in with two wickets in hand. Page 1.

New South Wales Environment Minister Pam Allan admitted yesterday she was wrong when she accused the Great Lakes Shire Council of ignoring a State Government order to clean up two sanitary depots, which she said caused the hepatitis A outbreak on the Stat's mid-North coast. However, Allan is refusing to apologise and is ignoring Opposition calls for her resignation. Page 3.
THE AGE

Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan has lashed out at Australia, accusing it of over-reacting and causing confusion leading up to the military revolt against his Government. Chan has also dismissed warnings from Australian Prime Minister John oward over the use of internationally-trained mercenaries to be used in the war on Bougainville. Page A1.

While Prime Minister John Howard yesterday supported the sacking of rebellious Papua New Guinean defence chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, he moved to warn Australia's neighbour of the consequences of using mercenaries on Bougainville. Page A1.

Trades Hall Council secretary Leigh Hubbard has criticised the Victorian Government's proposed sale of the 101-bus fleet Met Bus operation. On the eve of talks between unions and the Government, Hubbard said the sale was provocative and against State Trasport Minister Robin Cooper's pledge that the talks would begin on a clean slate. Page A1.

Despite his denial of knowledge on the weekend of the payout to Cheryl Harris, the former lover and chief of staff of Victorian Finance Minister Ian Smith, State Premier Jeff Kennett told Parliament yesterday that he had in fact "signed off" on the deal. Kennett has refused to state whether taxpayers' money was used in the settlement. Page A1.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
